title: What If Earth Stopped Rotating? One Sunrise a Year #shorts
description:
If Earth stopped rotating relative to distant stars, but its orbit and everything else were safely preserved, sunrise would return about once per year for many locations. This is an idealized thought experiment; a real instantaneous stop would be catastrophic. The Moon's orbit does not determine that solar day.

Sources:
NASA Earth Facts: https://science.nasa.gov/earth/facts/
NASA Spaceflight Reference Systems: https://science.nasa.gov/learn/basics-of-space-flight/chapter2-1/
NASA GSFC answer on Earth stopping: https://science.gsfc.nasa.gov/attic/cosmicopia.gsfc.nasa.gov/qa_earth.html
NASA Moon Facts: https://science.nasa.gov/moon/facts/

Original diagrams and computer-generated narration. Simplified physical assumptions are stated in the video.

scenes.say: What if Earth stopped spinning, but everything somehow slowed down safely?
Today the equator moves eastward at roughly seventeen hundred kilometres per hour.
A real instant stop would be catastrophic, so this is a simplified thought experiment.

scenes.say: Earth would still complete one orbit around the Sun in roughly three hundred sixty-five days.
Without axial spin, that orbit alone changes the Sun's direction in our sky.
Instead of sunrise every day, many places would see sunrise approximately once each year.
Around the equator, this means roughly six months of daylight and six months of darkness.
The Moon still circles Earth every twenty-seven days, but that does not set the solar day.
So in this thought experiment, the next sunrise could be a year away.
